narrative: The 2000s saw a resurgence of the natural hair movement among Black and African women, who were embracing their afro-textured locks in all their glory. The afro itself was a popular style, with its distinctive curl pattern and rounded shape becoming a symbol of pride and identity. Cornrows, a traditional hairstyle from Africa and the diaspora, were also gaining popularity, often styled in simple, straight lines or elaborate designs. Box braids, another protective style, became a staple among Black women, offering a convenient way to keep their hair healthy while still expressing themselves through fashion. Dreadlocks, locs, and Bantu knots were also on the rise, as women sought to celebrate their natural textures and reject the chemical treatments that had been prevalent in previous decades. The Jheri curl, once a popular style among Black Americans, was largely forgotten by this time, but its legacy lived on in the continued quest for self-expression and authenticity through hair culture.
